title: A good end that is not God himself is not enough
source_text: XVI. Neque est quod quis dicat ad Dei gloriam quodammodo referri actiones quae fiunt ob finem aliquem non malum, etiamsi agens de eo non cogitet. Exempli causa, quum aliquis verum Deum non cognoscens pecuniam egenti largitur, ut ei subveniat, ejusmodi actionem ad Dei gloriam spectare: quoniam omnis quae est in rebus creatis bonitas ad Deum per se spectat atque refertur. Nec enim ut actio in Dei gloriam fieri censenda sit, sufficit ut finis ejus res sit naturaliter bona, & proinde quae ex sua natura ad Deum referri queat. Alioqui qui laborat non alium ob finem, quam ut opes acquirat, posset dici in Dei gloriam laborare, siquidem opes per se res bona, non mala sunt. Et tamen labor ejusmodi proculdubio labor improbus est, & ad vitium non ad virtutem spectat.
pass_a_gloss: XVI. Nor is there reason why anyone should say that to God's glory in some way are referred actions which are done for some end not bad, even if the agent think not of it. For example's sake, when someone not knowing the true God bestows money on the needy, that he may relieve him, such an action looks to the glory of God: because all goodness which is in created things of itself looks and is referred to God. For in order that an action be deemed done to God's glory, it is not enough that its end be a thing naturally good, and therefore which by its nature can be referred to God. Otherwise he who labours for no other end, than that he may acquire riches, could be said to labour to God's glory, since riches in themselves are a good thing, not bad. And yet labour of that kind without doubt is wicked labour, and looks to vice not to virtue.
pass_b_english: Thesis XVI. Nor can anyone say that acts done for some end that is not bad are in some way referred to God's glory even if the agent does not think of it. Suppose, for example, that someone who does not know the true God gives money to a person in need in order to help him. It would be argued that such an act looks to God's glory, since all the goodness in created things looks to God of itself and is referred to him.

But for an act to be counted as done for God's glory, it is not enough that its end is something naturally good, which by its nature could be referred to God. Otherwise a man who works for no other end than to get rich could be said to work for God's glory, since wealth is in itself a good thing and not a bad one. Yet such work is undoubtedly wicked, and tends toward vice, not virtue.
